title: Desktop two-wheeled Wi-Fi/BLE rover (2S 18650, ESP32-C3, DRV8833, N20 drive)

brief.title: Small wheeled robot
brief.understanding: You want a robot, but haven't said yet what kind or what it should do. I've assumed a small two-wheeled rover you drive from your phone, since that is the simplest and cheapest starting point; the answers below will change the plan if you meant something else (arm, line follower, walker, etc.).

questions.question: What kind of robot do you want?
questions.why: This decides the motors, driver, frame and almost everything else.

questions.question: How should it be controlled?
questions.why: Sets which sensors and which controller are needed.

questions.question: How big should it be?
questions.why: Size sets motor power, battery size and cost.

questions.question: How should it be powered?
questions.why: Determines run time, weight and charging circuitry.

questions.question: What is your budget for parts for one robot?
questions.why: Limits the choice of motors, sensors and chassis.

requirements: Chassis about 15-20 cm long, total weight under 500 g
Two driven wheels plus one caster; top speed about 0.5 m/s on flat indoor floors
Powered by 2 x 18650 cells in series (7.4 V nominal, about 2000-2600 mAh)
Run time at least 60 minutes of continuous driving
Controlled from a phone over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, range at least 10 m indoors
Motor driver rated for at least 1 A continuous per motor
Power switch and low-battery cutoff or warning at about 6.4 V

blocks.name: Power
blocks.role: Two 18650 cells in a holder with protection and a power switch, stepped down to 3.3 V for the controller; cells are removed and charged in an external charger.
blocks.parts: 2 x protected 18650, 2S holder, 2S BMS board, 3.3 V buck regulator (e.g. MP1584 module)

blocks.name: Controller
blocks.role: Receives drive commands from the phone over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and sets motor speed and direction.

blocks.name: Motor driver
blocks.role: Switches battery power to the two motors forward and reverse with PWM speed control.

blocks.name: Motors and wheels
blocks.role: Two geared DC motors drive the wheels; steering is done by running them at different speeds.
blocks.parts: 2 x N20 6 V metal gear motors (about 200 RPM) with 43 mm wheels, ball caster

blocks.name: Chassis
blocks.role: Holds the motors, battery and electronics.
blocks.parts: Off-the-shelf 2WD acrylic chassis kit or 3D-printed plate

risks: The idea is very open: if you meant an arm, walker or something else, the motors, driver and cost change completely. Confirm the robot type first.
Motor start-up current can dip the supply and reset the controller. Add a bulk capacitor (470 uF or more) at the driver and check the 3.3 V rail under stall.
Lithium cells can be damaged or dangerous if shorted or over-discharged. Use protected cells or a BMS, and add a fuse.
A fresh 2S pack (8.4 V) exceeds the 6 V motor rating. Limit PWM duty in firmware to keep the average voltage at or below 6 V.

product.name: Desktop two-wheeled Wi-Fi/BLE rover (2S 18650, ESP32-C3, DRV8833, N20 drive)
product.summary: New design, nothing observed: every part is assumed. A two-piece printed (or moulded) shell holds one simple carrier PCB that takes the off-the-shelf modules from the brief: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1, DRV8833 breakout, MP1584 buck module and a 2S protection board, plus a PCB-mount 2x18650 holder reached through a top battery door. Two 18650 cells in series (7.4 V) feed the motor driver directly and the buck makes 3.3 V for the controller; two N20 gear motors with 43 mm wheels at the rear and a ball caster at the front give differential steering. Layout is scaled from the 18650 cell (18 x 65 mm, about 69 mm protected) and the N20 motor (10 x 12 x 24 mm); estimated mass is about 360 g and parts cost about 45-50 USD.
product.powerInput: 2 x 18650 Li-ion in series, 6.0-8.4 V (7.4 V nominal), about 2 A peak; cells are removed and charged in an external charger

parts.name: Lower chassis tray
parts.function: Structural base carrying the motors, caster, power switch and the bosses for the carrier PCB.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing for one unit; injection moulding in ABS at volume
parts.evidence: Designed for the brief: 15-20 cm chassis. Has motor cradles, shaft slots in the side walls, four 24 mm PCB bosses, corner screw bosses and a rear switch cut-out.
parts.unknowns: Wall could drop to 2 mm to save about 30 g; check stiffness on a first print.

parts.name: Top cover
parts.function: Closes the chassis and protects the electronics; has the battery door opening and the status LED hole.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing for one unit; injection moulding in ABS at volume
parts.evidence: Designed for the brief. Four deep screw wells at the corners, an 80 x 43 mm opening over the cell holder and a 5 mm hole for the LED.
parts.unknowns: A side slot for the dev board USB port could be added; it is not in this layout.

parts.name: Battery door
parts.function: Snap-on lid over the cell holder so the cells can be taken out for charging.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing; injection moulding at volume
parts.evidence: The brief says cells are removed and charged externally, so tool-free access is needed. Two hooks at one end, one snap latch at the other.

parts.name: Cover screws M3 x 12 self-tapping
parts.function: Hold the top cover to the tray corner bosses.
candidates: M3 x 12 pan-head thread-forming screw for plastic
parts.evidence: Design choice: pan-head screws sit in deep wells in the cover corners and bite into tray bosses.

parts.name: Carrier PCB
parts.function: Carries the cell holder and all modules and routes battery, 3.3 V and motor signals between them.
parts.process: Standard PCB fabrication, hand soldered through-hole
parts.evidence: Design choice: one 90 x 98 mm two-layer board (under the 100 mm low-cost fab limit) replaces loose wiring between the modules in the brief. Edge notch on the right side for the motor and switch leads.
parts.unknowns: Battery and motor traces should be at least 1.5 mm wide for 2 A; keep copper out from under the antenna end of the dev board.

parts.name: Carrier screws M2.5 x 6 self-tapping
parts.function: Fix the carrier PCB to the four tray bosses.
candidates: M2.5 x 6 pan-head thread-forming screw for plastic
parts.evidence: Design choice: two at the front corners, two beside the cell holder so the battery weight is supported.

parts.name: 2 x 18650 PCB-mount cell holder
parts.function: Holds the two cells and brings each cell's terminals to the carrier, which links them in series and gives the midpoint tap.
parts.material: PP or nylon with nickel-plated steel contacts
parts.evidence: The brief asks for a 2S holder; a PCB-mount type with separate contacts per cell gives the mid tap the 2S protection board needs.
parts.unknowns: Protected cells are 68-70 mm long and do not fit every holder; check the holder's maximum cell length or use unprotected cells and rely on the protection board.

parts.name: 18650 Li-ion cell, protected, 2600 mAh
parts.function: Energy source: two in series give 6.0-8.4 V and about 19 Wh.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: 2 x protected 18650, 2000-2600 mAh. At about 0.35 A average draw this gives several hours, well over the 60 minute target.
parts.unknowns: Use a matched pair from a reputable seller; capacity claims above 3600 mAh are fake.

parts.name: 2S Li-ion protection board
parts.function: Disconnects the pack on over-discharge (about 2.5 V per cell), over-charge and short circuit.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: 2S BMS board. Soldered flat to the carrier on B+, BM, B-, P+ and P- wire stubs.
parts.unknowns: Board size and trip current vary by seller; confirm the over-current trip is above 3 A so motor start does not cut power.

parts.name: 2-cell protection IC
parts.function: Monitors both cell voltages and the discharge current and drives the protection MOSFETs.
parts.evidence: Every 2S protection board of this type carries one such IC.
parts.unknowns: Read the top mark on the purchased board.

parts.name: Dual N-MOSFET protection switch
parts.function: Back-to-back MOSFET pair that opens the pack negative line when the protection IC trips.
parts.evidence: Standard partner to the protection IC on these boards.

parts.name: Power rocker switch
parts.function: Switches the protected battery output to the motor driver and the buck regulator.
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a power switch; a snap-in rocker rated 3 A or more is used because small PCB slide switches are only rated 0.1-0.3 A.

parts.name: Switch connector, JST-XH 2-pin
parts.function: Plugs the power switch leads into the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice so the carrier can be lifted out without desoldering.

parts.name: MP1584 buck converter module
parts.function: Steps the 6.0-8.4 V battery down to 3.3 V for the controller.
candidates: MP1584EN adjustable mini module, 22 x 17 mm
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: 3.3 V buck regulator, MP1584 module. Stands on four header pins.
parts.unknowns: The module is adjustable; output must be set to 3.3 V with a meter before the dev board is fitted.

parts.name: Buck module mounting pins
parts.function: Solder pins that carry IN+, IN-, OUT+ and OUT- and hold the module off the carrier.
candidates: 2.54 mm male pin header, cut to single pins
parts.evidence: Design choice: single 2.54 mm header pins at the module's four corner pads.

parts.name: MP1584EN step-down regulator
parts.function: 3 A, 28 V switching regulator at the heart of the buck module.
parts.evidence: Part number given in the brief.
parts.unknowns: Cheap modules often carry clone ICs; check ripple and output under 300 mA load.

parts.name: Buck inductor
parts.function: Energy storage inductor of the buck converter.
candidates: 8.2-15 uH shielded power inductor, 2 A or more
parts.evidence: Every MP1584 module carries a shielded inductor of about 6 x 6 mm.

parts.name: Output voltage trimmer
parts.function: Sets the buck output voltage; adjusted once to 3.3 V.
parts.evidence: Adjustable MP1584 modules have a single-turn trimmer in the feedback divider.
parts.unknowns: Lock with a drop of varnish after setting, or replace with fixed resistors.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 board
parts.function: Controller board: receives drive commands over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE and generates the motor PWM.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief. Plugged into two socket strips with the antenna end at the left wall, away from the cells and motors. Also carries an RGB LED on GPIO8.
parts.unknowns: The USB port faces the centre of the robot, so the cover comes off for the first flash; later updates can go over Wi-Fi (OTA).

parts.name: Dev board sockets, 1 x 15
parts.function: Let the dev board plug in and come out for reuse or replacement.
parts.evidence: Design choice: two 15-way 2.54 mm female strips on 22.86 mm row spacing.
parts.unknowns: Confirm the row spacing against the actual board before ordering the PCB.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 radio module
parts.function: RISC-V microcontroller with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE that runs the rover firmware.
parts.package: Castellated module with shield can, 13.2 x 16.6 mm overall
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief; it is the module fitted to the DevKitM-1.

parts.name: Module PCB antenna
parts.function: 2.4 GHz antenna for the phone link.
parts.evidence: Printed antenna on the end of the ESP32-C3-MINI-1; placed at the left wall with only plastic around it for the 10 m range target.
parts.unknowns: Range should be checked with the cover on and cells fitted; the cell cans are about 40 mm away.

parts.name: USB to UART bridge
parts.function: Lets a PC flash and debug the controller over the dev board USB port.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 carries a USB-UART bridge next to the USB connector.
parts.unknowns: Confirm on the purchased board revision.

parts.name: Dev board 3.3 V LDO
parts.function: Makes 3.3 V from USB 5 V when the board is powered from a PC; idle when running from the battery.
parts.evidence: All ESP32-C3 dev boards carry a 5 V to 3.3 V regulator.
parts.unknowns: Its output shares the 3V3 pin with the buck; see the safety note on USB and battery together.

parts.name: Dev board Micro-USB connector
parts.function: Programming and serial debug port.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 has a Micro-USB receptacle at the end opposite the antenna.

parts.name: Dev board Boot and Reset buttons
parts.function: Boot (GPIO9) selects download mode; Reset (EN) restarts the controller.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 has two tactile buttons; reachable only with the cover off.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual motor driver breakout
parts.function: Carrier for the dual H-bridge that drives both motors forward and reverse.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: DRV8833 or TB6612FNG breakout. Soldered to the carrier on two 8-pin header strips.
parts.unknowns: Pinout and size differ between makers; the carrier footprint must match the board actually bought.

parts.name: Driver breakout pin headers, 1 x 8
parts.function: Solder the driver breakout to the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice: standard 2.54 mm male strips on 10.16 mm row spacing.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual H-bridge driver
parts.function: Switches battery voltage to the two motors with PWM speed and direction control.
parts.evidence: Part number given in the brief. Rated 2.7-10.8 V and 1.5 A RMS per bridge, which meets the 1 A per motor requirement on a 2S pack.
parts.unknowns: Absolute maximum supply is 10.8 V; a full 2S pack at 8.4 V is inside it but a 3S pack is not.

parts.name: Motor supply bulk capacitor
parts.function: Holds up the motor rail during start and reversal so the controller does not brown out.
parts.evidence: Design choice: 470 uF 16 V next to the driver VM pin.

parts.name: Battery sense divider and LED resistors
parts.function: 100 k and 33 k divide the battery voltage to about 2.1 V for the ADC; 330 ohm limits the status LED current.
parts.evidence: Needed for the low-battery warning at 6.4 V and for the LED; values chosen for the ESP32-C3 ADC range.
parts.unknowns: Calibrate the ADC reading against a meter once; add 100 nF across the lower resistor if the reading is noisy.

parts.name: Status and low-battery LED
parts.function: Shows power and link state and flashes when the battery falls below 6.4 V.
parts.package: 5 mm through-hole with 14 mm nylon spacer
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a low-battery warning; a 5 mm LED on a spacer reaches through a hole in the top cover.

parts.name: Motor connectors, JST-XH 2-pin
parts.function: Plug the left and right motor leads into the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice so motors can be swapped and polarity reversed without soldering.

parts.name: Left N20 gear motor
parts.function: Drives the left wheel.
parts.package: N20 micro metal gear motor, 3 mm D-shaft
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: N20 6 V metal gear motor, about 200 RPM. With a 43 mm wheel that gives about 0.45 m/s. Shaft continues into the wheel hub.
parts.unknowns: Stall current of generic N20 motors varies from 0.4 to 1.6 A; measure it and solder 100 nF across the terminals.

parts.name: Right N20 gear motor
parts.function: Drives the right wheel.
parts.package: N20 micro metal gear motor, 3 mm D-shaft
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief; mirror of the left motor.

parts.name: Left wheel, 43 mm
parts.function: Left drive wheel, pressed on the motor D-shaft.
parts.material: ABS hub, rubber or silicone tyre
candidates: Generic 43 x 19 mm N20 wheel, 3 mm D-hole
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: 43 mm wheels. The common 43 x 19 mm N20 wheel with 3 mm D-bore is used.

parts.name: Right wheel, 43 mm
parts.function: Right drive wheel, pressed on the motor D-shaft.
parts.material: ABS hub, rubber or silicone tyre
candidates: Generic 43 x 19 mm N20 wheel, 3 mm D-hole
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief; mirror of the left wheel.

parts.name: Motor clamp strap
parts.function: Clamps each gearbox down into its cradle in the tray.
candidates: Pololu micro metal gearmotor bracket (item 989) as a bought alternative
parts.evidence: Design choice: flat printed strap over the gearbox with a screw each side.

parts.name: Clamp screws M2 x 6 self-tapping
parts.function: Hold the motor clamp straps to the tray.
candidates: M2 x 6 pan-head thread-forming screw for plastic
parts.evidence: Design choice: two per clamp into tray bosses.

parts.name: Front ball caster
parts.function: Third support point at the front that rolls in any direction.
candidates: Pololu ball caster with 3/8 inch metal ball (item 951)
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: ball caster. A 3/8 inch metal ball type is about 10 mm tall, matching the 10 mm ground clearance set by the 43 mm wheels.
parts.unknowns: Caster height must equal the clearance within about 1 mm; shim with the supplied spacers so the chassis sits level.

parts.name: Caster screws M2 x 6
parts.function: Fix the caster base to the underside of the tray.
candidates: M2 x 6 pan-head thread-forming screw for plastic
parts.evidence: Design choice: screwed from below through the caster flanges into tray floor bosses.

connections.label: Cell terminals (B+, BM, B-)
connections.evidence: Peak the path is sized for: both motors at 1 A plus the controller.

connections.label: B+, BM, B-
connections.medium: Carrier PCB traces, 1.5 mm or wider
connections.evidence: Series link and midpoint tap are made on the carrier.

connections.label: VBAT protected (P+)
connections.evidence: About 0.1 W lost in the protection MOSFETs at 2 A.

connections.label: VBAT to switch and back
connections.evidence: Switch is in the positive line after the protection board.

connections.label: VM (switched battery)
connections.medium: Wire back through J1, then carrier trace
connections.evidence: Peak share for the two motors.

connections.label: VIN (switched battery)
connections.medium: Wire back through J1, then carrier trace
connections.evidence: Input needed for 1 W out at about 90 percent efficiency.

connections.label: VM bulk decoupling
connections.evidence: Capacitor sits across VM and ground next to the driver.

connections.label: VBAT sense divider feed
connections.evidence: About 60 uA through 133 k; negligible in the budget.

connections.label: 3V3
connections.medium: Carrier PCB trace to the 3V3 socket pin
connections.evidence: ESP32-C3 transmit peaks near 0.28 A; average is about 0.1 A.

connections.label: 3V3
connections.evidence: Module is the main 3.3 V load; the rest is the LED and pull-ups.

connections.label: VM
connections.evidence: Same rail passed through the breakout pins.

connections.label: AOUT1/2 and BOUT1/2
connections.evidence: Both bridges together; PWM duty is capped so the 6 V motors see about 6 V average.

connections.label: Left motor
connections.medium: Twisted pair under the carrier, about 110 mm
connections.evidence: Sized for 1 A per motor as the brief requires; cruising draw is nearer 0.15 A.

connections.label: Right motor
connections.medium: Twisted pair under the carrier, about 60 mm
connections.evidence: Sized for 1 A per motor as the brief requires.

connections.label: VBUS (only when a PC is connected)
connections.evidence: Used for flashing on the bench; not part of the battery power budget.

connections.label: GND (P-)
connections.evidence: All returns go to the protected negative, never straight to the cell negative.

connections.label: AIN1, AIN2, BIN1, BIN2
connections.medium: Dev board sockets and carrier traces
connections.evidence: Four LEDC PWM outputs; GPIO4-7 suggested.

connections.label: nSLEEP
connections.evidence: Lets firmware disable the motors on low battery or lost link; GPIO10 suggested.

connections.label: nFAULT
connections.evidence: Reports over-current and thermal shutdown; GPIO3 with pull-up suggested.

connections.label: VBAT sense
connections.medium: Carrier trace to an ADC1 pin
connections.evidence: 6.4 V warning level reads about 1.59 V after the 100 k / 33 k divider; GPIO0 suggested.

connections.label: Status LED drive
connections.medium: Carrier trace through the 330 ohm resistor
connections.evidence: About 4 mA from a GPIO; GPIO1 suggested.

connections.label: D+ / D-
connections.evidence: Standard dev board programming path.

connections.label: TX, RX, auto-reset
connections.evidence: Standard dev board programming path.

connections.label: BOOT (GPIO9) and EN
connections.evidence: Standard dev board buttons.

connections.label: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi / Bluetooth LE
connections.evidence: Phone link required by the brief, 10 m indoors.

connections.label: Top cover to tray, 4 screws
connections.evidence: Design choice.

connections.label: Carrier PCB to tray bosses, 4 screws
connections.evidence: Design choice.

connections.label: Motor clamps to tray, 4 screws
connections.medium: Self-tapping screws through the clamp straps
connections.evidence: Design choice.

connections.label: Left wheel on 3 mm D-shaft
connections.evidence: Standard N20 wheel fixing.

connections.label: Right wheel on 3 mm D-shaft
connections.evidence: Standard N20 wheel fixing.

connections.label: Caster to tray floor, 2 screws
connections.evidence: Design choice.

connections.label: Battery door
connections.medium: Two hooks and a snap latch
connections.evidence: Design choice for tool-free cell removal.

controls.label: Power
controls.action: Connects the protected battery to the motor driver and the buck regulator; the controller boots, the status LED lights and the rover waits for the phone.

controls.label: Boot
controls.action: Held during reset it puts the controller in USB download mode for flashing; it does nothing in normal driving.

controls.label: Reset
controls.action: Restarts the controller; the motors stop and the status LED goes out while it is held.

unknowns: Nothing here is built or measured: all dimensions, currents and costs are design estimates.
The actual N20 motor stall current and speed are unknown until the motors are bought; they set the peak battery current and the top speed.
Whether protected 18650 cells (68-70 mm) fit the chosen PCB holder; if not, use unprotected cells with the 2S protection board.
Footprints of the DRV8833 breakout, the buck module and the 2S protection board differ between sellers; the carrier PCB must be drawn around the boards actually bought.
Wi-Fi/BLE range with the cover on and the cells fitted is untested against the 10 m target.
The dev board USB port is inside the cover; whether to add a side slot or rely on over-the-air updates is still open.
The buck feeds the dev board 3V3 pin in parallel with its own LDO output; feeding 5 V into the 5V pin instead would avoid that and should be considered.
GPIO numbers in the connections are suggestions and must be checked against the ESP32-C3 strapping pins (GPIO2, 8, 9).
Parts total of about 45-50 USD assumes generic motors and modules; branded equivalents (Pololu, Adafruit) would exceed the 60 USD budget.
verifySteps: Set the buck module to 3.30 V on a bench supply with a meter before the dev board is plugged in, then check it holds under a 300 mA load.
Measure the stall and free-running current of each motor at 6 V to confirm they stay under 1.5 A per DRV8833 bridge.
Measure the purchased modules and holder with calipers and correct the carrier PCB footprints and the dev board row spacing before ordering.
Drive on the floor at full command and log the battery voltage: confirm no brown-out resets on motor start and reversal.
Compare the ADC battery reading against a meter at 8.4 V and 6.4 V and adjust the firmware calibration and warning threshold.
Run a continuous drive test from full charge and time it against the 60 minute target; weigh the finished rover against the 500 g limit.
Walk the phone away indoors with the cover on to check the link holds at 10 m, and confirm the motors stop when the link drops.
Short the protected output briefly through a 5 A fuse to confirm the protection board trips and recovers.
safety: Lithium-ion cells: a short circuit can cause fire. Fit cells the right way round, never charge them in the robot, use a proper external charger and do not use damaged or unbranded cells.
Keep every return on the protected negative (P-); a wire from the cell negative to ground bypasses the protection board.
Set the adjustable buck to 3.3 V before fitting the dev board; as shipped it can output up to the battery voltage and will destroy the ESP32.
Do not have the USB cable and the battery switch on at the same time unless the 3V3 feed is changed, because the buck and the dev board regulator then fight on the same rail.
The DRV8833 absolute maximum is 10.8 V: never fit a 3S pack. Cap PWM duty at about 75 percent so the 6 V motors are not run at 8.4 V.
Stalled motors and the driver can get hot; firmware should cut drive on nFAULT, lost link or battery below about 6.0 V.
Wheels and gears can pinch fingers and catch hair; lift the rover off the floor when testing.

parts.evidence: Standard partner to the protection IC on these boards.

parts.name: Power rocker switch
parts.function: Switches the protected battery output to the motor driver and the buck regulator.
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a power switch; a snap-in rocker rated 3 A or more is used because small PCB slide switches are only rated 0.1-0.3 A.

parts.name: Switch connector, JST-XH 2-pin
parts.function: Plugs the power switch leads into the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice so the carrier can be lifted out without desoldering.

parts.name: MP1584 buck converter module
parts.function: Steps the 6.0-8.4 V battery down to 3.3 V for the controller.
candidates: MP1584EN adjustable mini module, 22 x 17 mm
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: 3.3 V buck regulator, MP1584 module. Stands on four header pins.
parts.unknowns: The module is adjustable; output must be set to 3.3 V with a meter before the dev board is fitted.

parts.name: Buck module mounting pins
parts.function: Solder pins that carry IN+, IN-, OUT+ and OUT- and hold the module off the carrier.
candidates: 2.54 mm male pin header, cut to single pins
parts.evidence: Design choice: single 2.54 mm header pins at the module's four corner pads.

parts.name: MP1584EN step-down regulator
parts.function: 3 A, 28 V switching regulator at the heart of the buck module.
parts.evidence: Part number given in the brief.
parts.unknowns: Cheap modules often carry clone ICs; check ripple and output under 300 mA load.

parts.name: Buck inductor
parts.function: Energy storage inductor of the buck converter.
candidates: 8.2-15 uH shielded power inductor, 2 A or more
parts.evidence: Every MP1584 module carries a shielded inductor of about 6 x 6 mm.

parts.name: Output voltage trimmer
parts.function: Sets the buck output voltage; adjusted once to 3.3 V.
parts.evidence: Adjustable MP1584 modules have a single-turn trimmer in the feedback divider.
parts.unknowns: Lock with a drop of varnish after setting, or replace with fixed resistors.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 board
parts.function: Controller board: receives drive commands over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE and generates the motor PWM.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief. Plugged into two socket strips with the antenna end at the left wall, away from the cells and motors. Also carries an RGB LED on GPIO8.
parts.unknowns: The USB port faces the centre of the robot, so the cover comes off for the first flash; later updates can go over Wi-Fi (OTA).

parts.name: Dev board sockets, 1 x 15
parts.function: Let the dev board plug in and come out for reuse or replacement.
parts.evidence: Design choice: two 15-way 2.54 mm female strips on 22.86 mm row spacing.
parts.unknowns: Confirm the row spacing against the actual board before ordering the PCB.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 radio module
parts.function: RISC-V microcontroller with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE that runs the rover firmware.
parts.package: Castellated module with shield can, 13.2 x 16.6 mm overall
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief; it is the module fitted to the DevKitM-1.

parts.name: Module PCB antenna
parts.function: 2.4 GHz antenna for the phone link.
parts.evidence: Printed antenna on the end of the ESP32-C3-MINI-1; placed at the left wall with only plastic around it for the 10 m range target.
parts.unknowns: Range should be checked with the cover on and cells fitted; the cell cans are about 40 mm away.

parts.name: USB to UART bridge
parts.function: Lets a PC flash and debug the controller over the dev board USB port.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 carries a USB-UART bridge next to the USB connector.
parts.unknowns: Confirm on the purchased board revision.

parts.name: Dev board 3.3 V LDO
parts.function: Makes 3.3 V from USB 5 V when the board is powered from a PC; idle when running from the battery.
parts.evidence: All ESP32-C3 dev boards carry a 5 V to 3.3 V regulator.
parts.unknowns: Its output shares the 3V3 pin with the buck; see the safety note on USB and battery together.

parts.name: Dev board Micro-USB connector
parts.function: Programming and serial debug port.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 has a Micro-USB receptacle at the end opposite the antenna.

parts.name: Dev board Boot and Reset buttons
parts.function: Boot (GPIO9) selects download mode; Reset (EN) restarts the controller.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 has two tactile buttons; reachable only with the cover off.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual motor driver breakout
parts.function: Carrier for the dual H-bridge that drives both motors forward and reverse.
parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: DRV8833 or TB6612FNG breakout. Soldered to the carrier on two 8-pin header strips.
parts.unknowns: Pinout and size differ between makers; the carrier footprint must match the board actually bought.

parts.name: Driver breakout pin headers, 1 x 8
parts.function: Solder the driver breakout to the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice: standard 2.54 mm male strips on 10.16 mm row spacing.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual H-bridge driver
parts.function: Switches battery voltage to the two motors with PWM speed and direction control.
parts.evidence: Part number given in the brief. Rated 2.7-10.8 V and 1.5 A RMS per bridge, which meets the 1 A per motor requirement on a 2S pack.
parts.unknowns: Absolute maximum supply is 10.8 V; a full 2S pack at 8.4 V is inside it but a 3S pack is not.

parts.name: Motor supply bulk capacitor
parts.function: Holds up the motor rail during start and reversal so the controller does not brown out.
parts.evidence: Design choice: 470 uF 16 V next to the driver VM pin.

parts.name: Battery sense divider and LED resistors
parts.function: 100 k and 33 k divide the battery voltage to about 2.1 V for the ADC; 330 ohm limits the status LED current.
parts.evidence: Needed for the low-battery warning at 6.4 V and for the LED; values chosen for the ESP32-C3 ADC range.
parts.unknowns: Calibrate the ADC reading against a meter once; add 100 nF across the lower resistor if the reading is noisy.

parts.name: Status and low-battery LED
parts.function: Shows power and link state and flashes when the battery falls below 6.4 V.
parts.package: 5 mm through-hole with 14 mm nylon spacer
parts.evidence: Brief asks for a low-battery warning; a 5 mm LED on a spacer reaches through a hole in the top cover.

parts.name: Motor connectors, JST-XH 2-pin
parts.function: Plug the left and right motor leads into the carrier.
parts.evidence: Design choice so motors can be swapped and polarity reversed without soldering.

parts.name: Left N20 gear motor

parts.evidence: Stated in the brief: N20 6 V metal gear motor, about 200 RPM. With a 43 mm wheel that gives about 0.45 m/s. Shaft continues into the wheel hub.
parts.unknowns: Stall current of generic N20 motors varies from 0.4 to 1.6 A; measure it and solder 100 nF across the terminals.

parts.name: Right N20 gear motor

controls.label: Power
controls.action: Connects the protected battery to the motor driver and the buck regulator; the controller boots, the status LED lights and the rover waits for the phone.

controls.label: Boot
controls.action: Held during reset it puts the controller in USB download mode for flashing; it does nothing in normal driving.

controls.label: Reset
controls.action: Restarts the controller; the motors stop and the status LED goes out while it is held.

unknowns: Nothing here is built or measured: all dimensions, currents and costs are design estimates.
The actual N20 motor stall current and speed are unknown until the motors are bought; they set the peak battery current and the top speed.
Whether protected 18650 cells (68-70 mm) fit the chosen PCB holder; if not, use unprotected cells with the 2S protection board.
Footprints of the DRV8833 breakout, the buck module and the 2S protection board differ between sellers; the carrier PCB must be drawn around the boards actually bought.
Wi-Fi/BLE range with the cover on and the cells fitted is untested against the 10 m target.
The dev board USB port is inside the cover; whether to add a side slot or rely on over-the-air updates is still open.
The buck feeds the dev board 3V3 pin in parallel with its own LDO output; feeding 5 V into the 5V pin instead would avoid that and should be considered.
GPIO numbers in the connections are suggestions and must be checked against the ESP32-C3 strapping pins (GPIO2, 8, 9).
Parts total of about 45-50 USD assumes generic motors and modules; branded equivalents (Pololu, Adafruit) would exceed the 60 USD budget.
verifySteps: Set the buck module to 3.30 V on a bench supply with a meter before the dev board is plugged in, then check it holds under a 300 mA load.
Measure the stall and free-running current of each motor at 6 V to confirm they stay under 1.5 A per DRV8833 bridge.
Measure the purchased modules and holder with calipers and correct the carrier PCB footprints and the dev board row spacing before ordering.
Drive on the floor at full command and log the battery voltage: confirm no brown-out resets on motor start and reversal.
Compare the ADC battery reading against a meter at 8.4 V and 6.4 V and adjust the firmware calibration and warning threshold.
Run a continuous drive test from full charge and time it against the 60 minute target; weigh the finished rover against the 500 g limit.
Walk the phone away indoors with the cover on to check the link holds at 10 m, and confirm the motors stop when the link drops.
Short the protected output briefly through a 5 A fuse to confirm the protection board trips and recovers.
safety: Lithium-ion cells: a short circuit can cause fire. Fit cells the right way round, never charge them in the robot, use a proper external charger and do not use damaged or unbranded cells.
Keep every return on the protected negative (P-); a wire from the cell negative to ground bypasses the protection board.
Set the adjustable buck to 3.3 V before fitting the dev board; as shipped it can output up to the battery voltage and will destroy the ESP32.
Do not have the USB cable and the battery switch on at the same time unless the 3V3 feed is changed, because the buck and the dev board regulator then fight on the same rail.
The DRV8833 absolute maximum is 10.8 V: never fit a 3S pack. Cap PWM duty at about 75 percent so the 6 V motors are not run at 8.4 V.
Stalled motors and the driver can get hot; firmware should cut drive on nFAULT, lost link or battery below about 6.0 V.
Wheels and gears can pinch fingers and catch hair; lift the rover off the floor when testing.
